section_summary: This section consists chiefly of late-1938 petitions from churches, civic groups, businesspeople, and other citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to halt American exports of arms, aircraft, petroleum, scrap metal, and other war materials to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation of war, while providing no authority to restrict most raw materials; several replies also describe the informal policy discouraging aircraft exports to countries bombing civilians. The section additionally contains export statistics, congressional inquiries, church resolutions advocating voluntary commercial pressure, and a May 1939 telegram denying that the Department had adopted an official position on pending neutrality legislation.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding the Community Church Peace Action Council resolution
subfiles.from: Donald G. Lothrop, Community Church of Boston
subfiles.about: Forwards a resolution adopted by the church's Peace Action Council concerning American economic assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lothrop forwards the Boston Community Church Peace Action Council's resolution, adopted without opposition, for Welles's consideration.

subfiles.title: Community Church resolution on neutrality and trade with Japan
subfiles.from: Peace Action Council of the Community Church of Boston
subfiles.to: President, Congress, Secretary of State, and federal authorities
subfiles.about: Calls for neutrality legislation distinguishing aggressors from victims and for restrictions on trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Council says American supplies make the U.S. Japan's main material ally, asking Congress to revise the Neutrality Act, executive limits on trade with Japan, and maximum Smoot-Hawley tariffs.

subfiles.title: The Community Church of Boston: What It Is and What It Does
subfiles.from: Community Church of Boston
subfiles.about: Explains the church's organization, principles, financing, and social-action councils.
subfiles.summary: The brochure describes a nonsectarian, democratically governed church devoted to universal religion, ethical life, cooperation, science, and social reconstruction. It explains the church's finances and lists its officers and directors. Its activities include cooperative, peace-action, civil-liberties, discussion, fellowship, and youth programs.

subfiles.title: Community Church Sunday service bulletin
subfiles.from: Community Church of Boston
subfiles.about: Provides the order of service, speaker program, church announcements, events, and hymns for December 11, 1938.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin announces Reinhold Niebuhr's address on the cultural foundations of democracy and fascism and lists musicians, hymns, and future speakers. It advertises church forums on anti-Semitism, cooperation, monopoly, Mexico, and fascism, along with membership and fundraising information. The final page prints the service hymns and a mailing-list form.

subfiles.title: Reply to Donald G. Lothrop
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Community Church resolution concerning the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Lothrop for the Peace Action Council's views and says the Department is closely studying the Far Eastern situation.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding the San Jose State College Y.W.C.A. resolution
subfiles.from: Mabel G. Grumbey, San Jose State College Y.W.C.A. Advisory Board
subfiles.about: Transmits a resolution seeking legislation to end sales of munitions and war-use raw materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grumbey forwards a San Jose State Y.W.C.A. resolution on Pacific Coast concern over America's share in Japan's war and asks legislation ending munitions and raw-material sales.

subfiles.title: Resolution concerning a Japanese munitions embargo
subfiles.from: Advisory Board, San Jose State College Y.W.C.A.
subfiles.to: President Franklin Roosevelt, Cordell Hull, Congress, and named California officials
subfiles.about: Demands a complete embargo on munition materials to Japan and regulation of comparable exports to other countries.
subfiles.summary: Resolution condemning Japanese aggression and calling for an immediate embargo on Japan, peacetime quotas elsewhere, and cooperation with civic groups.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mabel G. Grumbey
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the legal limits of the Neutrality Act in response to the Y.W.C.A. embargo resolution.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Mabel Grumbey: a presidential proclamation would bar arms to both China and Japan, other commodities are uncovered, and licensed arms since July 1937 were about $14.37 million to China and $10.90 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Charles M. Thomson's protest against the Neutrality Law
subfiles.from: Charles M. Thomson
subfiles.about: Argues that neutrality policy materially favors Japanese aggression and violates the spirit of American treaty commitments to China.
subfiles.summary: Charles Thomson protests the Neutrality Law: American oil, vehicles and scrap enable Japan's war while China cannot benefit equally; he invokes the Nine-Power Treaty and Open Door and urges a firm stand.

subfiles.title: Reply to Charles M. Thomson
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to Thomson's criticism by describing the Neutrality Act, export figures, aircraft policy, and U.S. statements under the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Green replies that no statute permits an embargo on oil, gasoline, vehicles or scrap, gives license totals, says aircraft licensing virtually ceased, and encloses the October 1937 press release and Brussels Conference material.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding the Roanoke ministers' resolution
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Sheppe Jr., Roanoke Virginia Ministers' Conference
subfiles.about: Transmits a resolution prompted by missionary reports that American munitions were enabling Japanese violence in China.
subfiles.summary: Sheppe forwards the Roanoke ministers' resolution, citing missionary reports of Japanese executions with American-supplied munitions.

subfiles.title: Roanoke Ministerial Association resolution
subfiles.from: Roanoke Ministerial Association
subfiles.to: President, Secretary of State, Virginia senators, and Sixth District congressman
subfiles.about: Petitions the President to proclaim a state of war between China and Japan and activate the neutrality laws.
subfiles.summary: Roanoke ministers say an actual but undeclared war exists, American supplies aid Japan, and ask the President to invoke the neutrality laws.

subfiles.title: Reply to Edwin S. Sheppe Jr.
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why existing neutrality legislation does not authorize the requested unilateral embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential proclamation would halt defined arms exports to China as well as Japan. He emphasizes that the act excludes other commodities and reports licensed arms-export totals for both countries. Copies of the Neutrality Act and the arms-traffic pamphlet are enclosed.

subfiles.title: Telegram on neutrality testimony and declining arms exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo; repeated to Peiping and Shanghai
subfiles.about: Denies that State Department officers had expressed an official view on pending neutrality legislation and reports the cessation of new arms-export licenses to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: no officer testified on pending neutrality bills, no authoritative ratio of American war materials in Japan's consumption exists, no arms licenses for Japan since December 12, 1938, and aircraft makers refused Japanese orders.

subfiles.title: Lyons Civic Club petition for an embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Isabelle Betts Hitchcock, Lyons Civic Club
subfiles.about: Petitions for an embargo on weapons, cotton, scrap iron, and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lyons Civic Club petition naming Japan aggressor, citing interference with American rights in China, and asking a stop to relevant exports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Isabelle Betts Hitchcock
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers the Lyons Civic Club petition with the Department's standard explanation of neutrality law and export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential war proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while the act does not authorize restrictions on other commodities. He reports licensed arms exports since July 1937 and encloses the Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Mrs. E. L. Quackenbush
subfiles.about: Raises concern about American scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Heavily degraded letter on scrap-iron exports to Japan requesting constructive action.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. Quackenbush
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: States that scrap iron falls outside the commodities which the Neutrality Act permits the President to embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that the act authorizes restrictions only on defined arms, ammunition, and implements of war. Because scrap iron is expressly outside that category, no existing statute permits its prohibition to Japan or another foreign country.

subfiles.title: E. C. Roworth's letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: E. C. Roworth
subfiles.about: Urges the government to stop supplying Japan with aircraft, manufacturing licenses, scrap iron, and other war materials.
subfiles.summary: Roworth quotes a Business Week report about Japanese acquisition of American aircraft designs, engines, and technical assistance. He argues that helping Japan's war machine increases the danger of a future war and the cost of American rearmament. He suggests using federal purchasing power to pressure manufacturers.

subfiles.title: E. C. Roworth's duplicate letter to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: E. C. Roworth
subfiles.about: Sends the President the same appeal to prevent American assistance to Japan's military aviation and broader war machine.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats Roworth's quotation about Japanese purchases of American aircraft designs and licenses. It urges government pressure on manufacturers and argues that continued assistance will increase American defense costs and the possibility of war.

subfiles.title: Consolidated reply to E. C. Roworth
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Roworth's letters to Hull and Roosevelt with an explanation of export law and the policy discouraging aviation sales to bombing states.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges both letters and explains that the Neutrality Act would restrict arms to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation. Other commodities remain outside executive embargo authority. He reports export-license totals and says licensing of aircraft and aircraft supplies has virtually ceased under the civilian-bombing policy.

subfiles.title: Roworth follow-up to Joseph C. Green
subfiles.from: E. C. Roworth
subfiles.about: Thanks Green and advocates revised legislation that discriminates between aggressor and non-aggressor states.
subfiles.summary: Roworth welcomes reported progress limiting munitions shipments to Japan and hopes laws are amended to restrict aggressors, arguing it could save billions in defense costs.

subfiles.title: Board of Bishops appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: H. Lester Smith, Board of Bishops of the Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: Urges the President to stop American citizens from supplying Japan with materials used to devastate China.
subfiles.summary: Board of Bishops condemns Japanese bombing and invasion, ashamed that American oil, scrap and munitions sustain it, and asks why Americans should arm both themselves and Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Bishop H. Lester Smith
subfiles.from: Walton Moore for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that existing law does not permit executive restrictions on the raw materials named by the bishops.
subfiles.summary: Moore says a presidential proclamation would embargo listed arms to China as well as Japan. Petroleum, scrap iron, steel, cotton, and copper are not within the statutory arms list, so the President and Secretary lack authority to prohibit them. The reply also supplies licensed arms-export totals for both belligerents.

subfiles.title: Gerald P. Nye request for export and German engine data
subfiles.from: Gerald P. Nye, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Requests monthly China-Japan war-material export figures and information on German production of Pratt & Whitney-licensed engines.
subfiles.summary: Gerald Nye asks for an eighteen-month comparison of war-related exports to China and Japan and for data on Bavarian Motor Works production under a Pratt & Whitney license.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Gerald P. Nye
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Supplies export bulletins and arms-license statistics while addressing Nye's question about German aircraft-engine production.
subfiles.summary: Green sends Nye Commerce bulletins and an arms-license table, attributing declining Japanese authorizations to the policy against supplying states that bomb civilians.

subfiles.title: Monthly arms-export license tabulation for China and Japan
subfiles.from: Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Lists monthly values of licensed arms, ammunition, and implements-of-war exports to China and Japan from July 1937 through November 1938.
subfiles.summary: Monthly table of arms-export licenses to China and Japan, totaling about $14.37 million and $10.79 million.

subfiles.title: Centerville Methodist Episcopal Church resolution
subfiles.from: Algernon S. Gallup, Centerville Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: Reports a church conference resolution opposing war-material exports to Japan and low tariffs on Japanese imports.
subfiles.summary: Centerville Methodist conference resolution: American supplies feed Japanese munitions and low tariffs displace American workers; it asks Hull to end both.

subfiles.title: Reply to Algernon S. Gallup
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds to the Centerville church resolution with the Department's explanation of neutrality law and arms exports.
subfiles.summary: Yost explains that a presidential proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while other commodities fall outside the act. He provides licensed-export totals and encloses the Joint Resolution and International Traffic in Arms pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Waverley Club resolutions and petition
subfiles.from: David Snedden, Waverley Club of Palo Alto
subfiles.about: Transmits a unanimous petition asking the government to end American traffic in materials supporting Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: The club condemns Japan's treaty violations, bombing of undefended cities, and destruction of civilian institutions. It expresses shame that American planes, shells, oil, trucks, and scrap iron aid the invasion. The petition asks the President and Congress to use every practicable direct or indirect means to terminate the traffic.

subfiles.title: Reply to David Snedden
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains legal limits on an embargo and describes the near cessation of aircraft-export licenses to bombing states.
subfiles.summary: Yost says the Neutrality Act would embargo defined arms to both China and Japan only after a presidential proclamation and does not cover other commodities. He supplies licensed-export totals and states that aircraft and aircraft-supply licensing has virtually ceased because of Japan's bombing of civilians.

subfiles.title: Margaret M. Ward's appeal to stop shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Margaret M. Ward, St. John's Cathedral
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government can halt materials essential to Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: Margaret Ward calls the slaughter of women and children appalling, charges American profit-seeking sustains it, and asks Hull to act.

subfiles.title: Reply to Margaret M. Ward
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act's limits and notes congressional proposals to revise neutrality legislation.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that invoking the act would embargo arms to China as well as Japan and that commodities beyond the statutory arms list cannot be prohibited administratively. He provides licensed-export totals for both countries. The letter notes that several bills to revise neutrality law had been introduced in Congress.

subfiles.title: Instruction to draft replies to attached correspondence
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Directs Hornbeck to prepare appropriate replies for Welles's signature to two attached letters.
subfiles.summary: The brief Under Secretary's memorandum forwards two pieces of correspondence. It asks Hornbeck to draft responses for Welles to sign.

subfiles.title: J. P. Welles letter on Germany and the Sino-Japanese conflict
subfiles.from: J. P. Welles
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Praises Welles's stand against German atrocities while urging stronger action against Japanese conduct and exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. P. Welles contrasts the response to Nazi abuses with restraint toward Japan, citing missionary reports, and asks an effective block on oil, gasoline and scrap-iron shipments.

subfiles.title: Reply to J. P. Welles
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: States that the executive branch lacks authority to prohibit the commodities named in the correspondent's letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks the writer, saying the executive cannot prohibit the listed exports and policy must operate within legislation.

subfiles.title: Senate referral of J. E. Joseph's inquiry
subfiles.from: Office of Senator Josh Lee, United States Senate
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent inquiry for favorable consideration and a report.
subfiles.summary: The Senate office transmits the accompanying communication to Hull. It requests a report to be returned with the enclosure.

subfiles.title: J. E. Joseph inquiry about junk-metal sales
subfiles.from: J. E. Joseph
subfiles.about: Asks whether the United States permits junk-metal sales to Japan while refusing comparable sales to China.
subfiles.summary: J. E. Joseph asks whether claims that American junk iron and metals feed Japanese war production are correct and whether China is denied the same materials.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Josh Lee concerning junk metals
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the Neutrality Act does not authorize restrictions on junk iron or metals shipped to China or Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department says the act is limited to defined arms, ammunition, and implements of war and excludes junk metal. No statute permits a general prohibition on such exports to Japan, China, or other countries, apart from the law governing tin-plate scrap. Joseph's letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Federal Council of Churches resolution
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles and Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Summarizes the origin and intended implementation of a church-council resolution advocating moral pressure on exporters to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports Mr. Barnes supplied the Federal Council of Churches' December 9 resolution, a voluntary-pressure compromise after a legal embargo proposal failed.

subfiles.title: Federal Council of Churches action on war supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: Federal Council of the Churches of Christ in America
subfiles.to: Churches, investors, commercial enterprises, and Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Calls for voluntary discontinuance of essential war-material sales to Japan and investor pressure on participating companies.
subfiles.summary: Federal Council of Churches resolution condemning Japanese aggression, praising aircraft firms refusing contracts, urging sellers of oil, trucks and scrap to sacrifice profits, and asking churches to examine investments.

subfiles.title: Omaha and Douglas County Council of Churches resolution
subfiles.from: W. F. Cozad and A. L. Cole, Omaha and Douglas County Council of Churches
subfiles.about: Protests American participation in Japan's invasion of China and urges prohibition of war-supply shipments.
subfiles.summary: Omaha and Douglas County Council of Churches says destruction in China involved American-made shells, Japan couldn't continue without U.S. supplies, and asks officials to prohibit shipments.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. F. Cozad
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers the Omaha church resolution by explaining the Neutrality Act and providing arms-export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost to W. F. Cozad: a proclamation would bar defined arms to both China and Japan, no authority covers other commodities, with license totals and enclosed pamphlets.
